Twenty-person ultrasound pilot supports feasibility, not efficacy

In a single-arm pilot of 20 amyloid-PET-positive patients with prodromal or mild Alzheimer disease, four weeks of low-intensity ultrasound caused no severe adverse events or MRI-detected hemorrhage, microbleeding or edema; executive-test and NPI scores improved, but MMSE, attention and quality of life did not, and the uncontrolled design precludes efficacy claims.

Early signal•Peer-reviewed prospective interventional pilot trial•September 29, 2026

Twenty-person ultrasound pilot supports feasibility, not efficacy

In a single-arm pilot of 20 amyloid-PET-positive patients with prodromal or mild Alzheimer disease, four weeks of low-intensity ultrasound caused no severe adverse events or MRI-detected hemorrhage, microbleeding or edema; executive-test and NPI scores improved, but MMSE, attention and quality of life did not, and the uncontrolled design precludes efficacy claims.

Key quantitative results: No severe adverse events occurred, and post-treatment MRI showed no intracerebral hemorrhage, microbleeding or brain edema in the 20 treated participants.

Clinical TrialsExperimental treatment safety

Added September 30, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/13872877261493067; PMID:42808496

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The trial establishes that a repeated four-week bilateral frontal and temporal ultrasound protocol was feasible in a very small biomarker-confirmed early-AD group, without the MRI safety signals reported in the abstract. Nominal improvements in Trail Making and neuropsychiatric scores are hypothesis-generating only: there was no sham arm, the sample was 20, several outcomes were tested, and global cognition, attention and quality of life did not significantly change.

Study design

Twenty people with amyloid-PET-positive prodromal Alzheimer disease or mild Alzheimer dementia received low-intensity ultrasound targeting bilateral frontal and temporal regions three times weekly for four weeks. Neurological examinations and brain MRI assessed safety. Exploratory outcomes included Trail Making Test-Black & White parts A and B, Attention Questionnaire Scale, Korean Quality of Life, MMSE and Neuropsychiatric Inventory; resting-state functional MRI was analyzed in a subset.

Key quantitative results

  • No severe adverse events occurred, and post-treatment MRI showed no intracerebral hemorrhage, microbleeding or brain edema in the 20 treated participants.
  • Trail Making Test-Black & White part A decreased from 105.3±63.3 to 84.2±46.6 seconds (p=0.012), and part B decreased from 280.1±139.9 to 212.8±59.7 seconds (p=0.038).
  • Neuropsychiatric Inventory score decreased from 9.8±14.7 to 4.5±8.8 (p=0.006), while MMSE, Attention Questionnaire Scale and Korean Quality of Life did not change significantly.

What changed

A September 29 prospective report provides the first small repeated-protocol feasibility and short-term safety signal for this low-intensity ultrasound approach in amyloid-PET-confirmed early Alzheimer disease.

Strength of evidence

Very low efficacy certainty and preliminary safety evidence from 20 treated participants. The single-arm design, short exposure and follow-up, multiple exploratory outcomes, large baseline variability and lack of sham control preclude causal or durable-benefit inference.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The protocol merits randomized, sham-controlled evaluation but should not change clinical management. The absence of serious events in 20 participants cannot establish uncommon or longer-term safety, and nominal cognitive or behavioral changes may reflect practice, expectation or regression-to-the-mean effects.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to emerging nonpharmacologic therapeutic development and to counseling stakeholders about the difference between feasibility/safety signals and evidence of clinical benefit.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The intervention remains experimental. The study establishes neither authorization nor routine availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did the study show that ultrasound treats Alzheimer disease?
No. Every participant received the intervention, so practice effects, expectation effects and natural variation cannot be separated from treatment effects.
Why is this Clinical Trials rather than Biomarkers?
The central question was an interventional ultrasound protocol. Amyloid PET established eligibility; the study did not evaluate biomarker measurement, interpretation or implementation.
Is the safety evidence sufficient for routine use?
No. Twenty participants and four weeks of treatment can support feasibility but cannot characterize uncommon events, longer-term risk or outcomes outside the study protocol.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Only 20 participants
  • No randomized or sham-control group
  • Four-week treatment period with limited follow-up
  • Multiple exploratory outcomes without evidence of multiplicity control in the abstract
  • No significant change in MMSE, attention or quality of life
  • Insufficient size to estimate uncommon or delayed adverse events

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Park BY, Jo SW, Park TY, et al. Feasibility and safety of repeated low-intensity ultrasound in amyloid PET-positive early Alzheimer's disease: A prospective pilot study. J Alzheimers Dis. Published online September 29, 2026. doi:10.1177/13872877261493067.
